stories.headline: Tracking WNBA MVP race, awards: Time to vote for the winners
stories.summary: A'ja Wilson (MVP) and Olivia Miles (ROY) are shoo-ins. A Golden State duo is among our other award winners.
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Alexa Philippou and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
With four days remaining in the regular season -- and official ballots due Friday -- it's time to vote on this year's WNBA awards.

Throughout the 2026 campaign, ESPN has tracked the front-runners and top contenders for MVP, Rookie of the Year, Defensive Player of the Year, Most Improved Player, Sixth Player of the Year and Coach of the Year. Now, Michael Voepel, Alexa Philippou, Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland make their final selections.

Among our panel, there's little intrigue for the league's biggest honor: A'ja Wilson looks poised to win her fifth MVP and fourth in five years, adding to her already-record-setting haul. Even less of a debate was ESPN's pick for Rookie of the Year, Minnesota Lynx star Olivia Miles, who also is our runner-up for MVP.

Here's where we also land on the rest of the league's top awards.

Jump to:

MVP | Rookie of Year | Defensive Player of Year

Most Improved | Sixth Player | Coach of Year

MVP

Kendra Andrews: A'ja Wilson, Las Vegas Aces

Kareem Copeland: A'ja Wilson, Las Vegas Aces

Alexa Philippou: A'ja Wilson, Las Vegas Aces

Michael Voepel: A'ja Wilson, Las Vegas Aces

ESPN's pick: A'ja Wilson, Las Vegas Aces

Last season, Wilson became the WNBA's first four-time MVP. If she wins a fifth MVP, she'll enter even more rarified air in American professional team sports history.

The all-time leader in MVP awards in the NHL is Wayne Gretzky, who won the Hart Trophy nine times, including eight in a row. Barry Bonds (seven) leads MLB players, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (six) leads the NBA and Peyton Manning (five) leads the NFL.

Wilson's Aces are the defending WNBA champions. They are seeking their fourth title, and Wilson has been at the heart of it all since being drafted No. 1 in 2018. This season, she leads the WNBA in scoring (26.1 points per game), blocks (2.0 per game), player efficiency rating (32.4) and win shares (8.6). She ranks fourth in rebounding (9.3 per game).

Wilson, who turned 30 in August, has dealt with back issues this season that kept her from playing in the FIBA World Cup. But overall, she has remained a dominant force in the league. That's even more impressive when you consider the challengers for this award during Wilson's career, including this season. -- Voepel

ESPN's runner-up: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

You could take your pick of strong contenders, including the Indiana Fever's Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell, the New York Liberty's Breanna Stewart and the Atlanta Dream's Rhyne Howard. The case for Miles: The point guard took the keys to the Lynx's offense as a rookie with superstar forward Napheesa Collier out injured until July 22. Miles is averaging 19.8 points, 6.0 assists and 4.7 rebounds for the Lynx, who have the league's best record. Candace Parker was the only rookie to also win the WNBA's MVP award, in 2008, so it says something for a first-year player to even be in the conversation. -- Voepel

Rookie of the Year

Andrews: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

Copeland: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

Philippou: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

Voepel: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

ESPN's pick: Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx

From day one, Miles grabbed the lead for Rookie of the Year and never let go. In her debut, she dropped 21 points, eight assists, three rebounds and two steals -- and immediately proved she would be a force in the league. The No. 3 draft pick set the WNBA record for points scored by a rookie, and she is in the conversation to be named MVP.

Miles has been the best player on the best team throughout the season and ranks in the top 10 in the league in points and assists per game while being in the top five for rebounds per game by a guard. On Friday, Miles registered her seventh game of 20 points, five assists and five rebounds; that passed Tamika Catchings for the second most by a rookie in WNBA history and only trails Caitlin Clark (14).

Miles won every Rookie of the Month Award given by the league this season. In July, she became the 10th player in league history to record 30-plus points, eight-plus assists and eight-plus rebounds in a single game. Miles -- so dominant that we aren't even selecting a runner-up -- was instantly one of the best passers and quickly showed the ability to get to the rim at will. Defenders learned over the course of the campaign that she also can shoot from behind the arc; her eight treys on June 4 set a league record for rookies. -- Copeland

Defensive Player of the Year

Andrews: Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries

Copeland: Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries

Philippou: Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries

Voepel: Angel Reese, Atlanta Dream

ESPN's pick: Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries

The Valkyries have been the WNBA's best defensive team this season, allowing 74.8 PPG. They are the only team holding foes to fewer than 80 PPG, and opponents have shot just 41.5% from the field against them. Williams, in her first season with Golden State, has been one of the biggest keys to that effort.

The 5-foot-11 forward can guard players of all sizes. She is second in defensive rating (99.1) and one of four Valkyries players who are in the top five in that category. Williams and guard Veronica Burton, also a candidate for this award, lead the Valkyries in averaging 1.6 steals apiece. -- Voepel

ESPN's runner-up: Angel Reese, Atlanta Dream

Atlanta is second to Golden State in defensive rating (104.9), and Reese has improved her defense enough in her third WNBA season to be considered for this award. At 6-foot-4, she is a strong post defender and an elite rebounder who also can guard on the perimeter and cut off passing lanes. Reese leads the WNBA in defensive win shares (3.2) and is fourth in defensive rating (100.4).

Wilson, a three-time WNBA DPOY, is also in contention for this honor. -- Voepel

Most Improved Player

Andrews: Jessica Shepard, Dallas Wings

Copeland: Shakira Austin, Washington Mystics

Philippou: Jessica Shepard, Dallas Wings

Voepel: Jessica Shepard, Dallas Wings

ESPN's pick: Jessica Shepard, Dallas Wings

Players tend to end up in the Most Improved conversation in a few different ways. They might finally be healthy, enjoying an expanded role, thriving in a new system or benefitting from the work they put into the offseason. Shepard's successful campaign is largely a product of having more opportunity with the Wings; her 31.6 minutes per game are a career high and 10 more than she averaged last year with Minnesota. But even in her best stretches with the Lynx, it wasn't obvious she'd one day become such a critical, go-to player who a playoff-bound team -- and, in the longer term, a championship-minded one -- can build around and play through.

Shepard is on track to become the first player to average at least 10 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a season. (Candace Parker did so in 2015, but in only 16 games.) And while Alyssa Thomas is still the league's triple-double queen, Shepard leads the WNBA this season in that category with five. And Shepard's 23 double-doubles are second most, behind Angel Reese. That's all from a second-round draft pick who turned 30 this year and never averaged more than 8.1 points per game prior to this season. -- Philippou

ESPN's runner-up: Shakira Austin, Washington Mystics

Austin has been known for her defense and athleticism since entering the league, but her offensive game took a significant step forward as she helped the Mystics return to the playoffs for the first time since 2023. Her scoring average has increased by more than four points over that of last year to rank in the top 15 in the league, and she has averaged three more rebounds to rank in the top five.

Finally healthy, Austin has displayed an expanded offensive repertoire with an ability to put the ball on the floor and attack from the perimeter with her 6-foot-5 frame. The No. 3 draft pick in 2023 ranks in the top 11 in defensive win shares for the No. 2 scoring defense in the league. -- Copeland

Sixth Player of the Year

Andrews: Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries

Copeland: Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries

Philippou: Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries

Voepel: Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries

ESPN's pick: Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries

Few players have provided as big a spark off the bench as Salaun has for Golden State. In 22.9 minutes per game, she has become the team's second-best scorer, averaging 12.9 points. That's also the second-best scoring mark in the league among bench players seeing at least 20 minutes per game.

Salaun has established herself as one of the premier knockdown shooters in the WNBA, shooting 39.7% from 3 on 6.1 attempts per game, which is the best percentage among bench players averaging at least five 3-point shots.

The Valkyries outscore opponents by 4.7 points when Salaun is on the floor -- the second-best net rating among bench players averaging at least 20 minutes -- as she has made a habit of providing momentum-shifting plays. -- Andrews

ESPN's runner-up: Marine Johannes, New York Liberty

Johannes started for New York early on, but she has come off the bench in all but two games since June 19. She has been one of the Liberty's most dependable reserves, averaging 8.7 points, 2.1 rebounds and 2.4 assists. -- Voepel

Coach of the Year

Andrews: Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx

Copeland: Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx

Philippou: Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx

Voepel: Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx

ESPN's pick: Cheryl Reeve, Minnesota Lynx

The Lynx have been a regular-season powerhouse for several consecutive years, but what Reeve has led them to this season feels different. Without Collier, their superstar forward, for much of the year, Reeve has coached rookie sensation Miles into one of the best and most impactful players in the league and established a new identity with a roster that started the campaign with just two returning players.

The Lynx have had the league's best record all season and are trying to clinch the No. 1 seed heading into the playoffs. They have the third-best offense (112.5 offensive rating) and the third-best defense (103.7 defensive rating).

In July, Collier told ESPN that if this season has proved anything, it's to never count out Reeve. Yes, she is the all-time winningest coach in league history, but remember that entering this season, some questioned how Minnesota would stay afloat with so much roster turnover and Collier sidelined indefinitely. Reeve has overachieved, outperformed expectations and once again led Minnesota to be a top contender. -- Andrews

ESPN's runner-up: Sydney Johnson, Washington Mystics

The Mystics were supposed to be in a methodical rebuild with a new draft-and-develop strategy that could take some time to return to the postseason. In Year 2, Johnson led Washington to the playoffs as the youngest team in league history to make the postseason. With six first-round picks from the past two drafts, Johnson has molded Washington into a defensive force as the No. 2 scoring defense in the league. He adapted when the big three of Austin, Kiki Iriafen and Sonia Citron requested that Johnson be more demanding, and he put more of an emphasis on wins and losses after 2025 was focused on building a cultural foundation. The Mystics' 26 wins this season matches that of their 2019 WNBA championship team for the most in franchise history. Washington is back in the playoffs for the first time since 2023. -- Copeland

stories.headline: Toto Wolff warned Michael Masi against being 'stubborn, arrogant' before F1 2021 title controversy
stories.summary: Toto Wolff has claimed he repeatedly warned Michael Masi not to be "stubborn" or "arrogant" during the 2021 Formula 1 season.
stories.body:
Toto Wolff has claimed he repeatedly warned Michael Masi not to be "stubborn" or "arrogant" during the 2021 Formula 1 season, saying he tried to guide the former race director before the controversial title-deciding Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Masi broke the rules he was supposed to enforce around the safety car, forcing a final-lap restart at the end of the title decider between Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen.

Verstappen passed Hamilton on the lap to claim his first championship and to deny the then-Mercedes driver what would have been a record eighth title.

Wolff spoke about the controversy on the High Performance Podcast in 2024, where he was asked what the overriding emotions were at the time.

"Angry. Not anything [like] depressed or sad. Just angry," Wolff said. "Angry that an individual to take an eighth championship away from the best driver in the world by a decision."

Masi was removed from his role after the season and has not been back in a prominent motor racing position since.

Wolff went on to state that Masi, who joined SRO Motorsports Australia last week as head of sporting operations, is no longer relevant in the sport.

He explained that he had tried to help Masi and offered him counsel through the season and that the outcome was avoidable.

"I really tried to speak to Michael and guide him all along the year," Wolff said. "I said, 'listen I've been in the sport for a long time, listen to the drivers, don't always be stubborn in your decision making, don't be arrogant.'

"I tried that for the good of the sport, and obviously also for us as a team not to be vulnerable to situations that could be totally detrimental.

"So in that sense, this is just what happened is inexcusable. You could say empathy should make me realise how he feels. I realise how it feels. And I know that's not good, it's bad, but he could have thought about it all year long, when people, not only me, tried to support him in the right way.

Saunders: I raced against Verstappen ... for 10 seconds

- Hamilton clears the air on Ferrari replacements

- Norris: Monaco GP 2027 sprint 'exciting' for fans

"So sometimes you have to just realise that someone is just doing his own thing or taking his own decisions. So for me, I don't care about it anymore. Now you and I speak about it and we waste three minutes of our time, but he has no relevance."

Although Wolff said he is over it emotionally, there are regular reminders about what the team lost that day.

"Every week," he said when asked how often he thinks about it. "I mainly think about it because I think Lewis deserved to be the greatest of all time with eight world championship titles. And you can argue all along about that year.

"I think Max and Lewis were deserving champions. There were instances during the year where Max lost some points that he shouldn't have lost. You look at the crash in Monza both of them had. So both deserving champions, but on that particular afternoon in Abu Dhabi, it was unfair."

stories.headline: Dreyer outduels Messi as San Diego hands Miami 4th straight draw
stories.summary: Lionel Messi scored his 101st goal for Inter Miami CF, but Anders Dreyer scored twice for San Diego FC, as the teams played to a 2-2 draw on Sunday night.
stories.body:
MIAMI -- Lionel Messi scored his 101st goal for Inter Miami CF, but Anders Dreyer scored twice for San Diego FC, as the teams played to a 2-2 draw on Sunday night.

It was Inter Miami's fourth consecutive draw in MLS play as new manager Kily González oversaw his first league game in charge of the club and cut a frustrated figure after conceding a late goal to drop points.

"We've been here for four days and haven't been able to train properly. Defensively, we really need to be much stronger," González said after the game. "We can't commit these defensive horrors, they come at a high cost. That final situation shouldn't have happened. It's surreal to be in a position to win the game, yet nearly lose it.

"We only avoided defeat because our goalkeeper saved us."

Dreyer gave San Diego a 1-0 lead in the 12th minute, capitalizing on a through ball from Jeppe Tverskov before deftly chipping over goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair.

Messi answered in the 24th with his 20th league goal of the season. His free kick from the right side went untouched through the penalty area and into the far side of the net, four days after he scored his 100th goal for Inter Miami in a 2-0 win over Mexican side Cruz Azul in the Campeones Cup.

"I think the Campeones Cup might have had an unconscious effect, especially in the first half, leading to a bit of complacency," González added. "These are factors that are part of football. At a club where we are obliged to win every match we play, we have to rise to the occasion. We made significant adjustments at halftime to get the team flowing and ensure we stayed compact, keeping the lines tight so we wouldn't suffer the way we did in the first half."

The goal was Messi's eighth from a free kick since entering the league in 2023, more than any other player in MLS during that time span.

Luis Suárez put Miami ahead in the 74th minute as Miami looked set to leapfrog New England into second place in the Eastern Conference, but Dreyer scored his second of the night eight minutes later with another fine finish -- this time from a ball over the top of the Herons' backline.

Miami is now in third place with a record of 12-4-10 with 46 points -- 11 behind first-place Nashville.

"But anyway, we have to keep going," González said. "On the positive side, we did some good things, but I need to fine-tune the defensive side because that's what really worries me most."

Earlier Sunday, FIFA announced that the final phase of the 2027 FIFA Women's Champions Cup will be played at Inter Miami's home of Nu Stadium in January. FIFA Chief Football Officer Jill Ellis spoke at halftime about bringing the competition to Miami.

"I think we've seen that this city loves its football. We've seen it this past summer with the World Cup," Ellis said. "I think it's time to bring a major women's tournament here to Miami. I think it's exciting."

Miami returns to MLS play next Sunday on the road against the Columbus Crew, while San Diego is also on the road with a game against Austin FC on Saturday.

ESPN writer Lizzy Becherano contributed to this report, while information from The Associated Press was also used.

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

stories.headline: NRL investigating after referee peppered with rubbish
stories.summary: Warriors great Shaun Johnson has labelled footage of fans throwing projectiles at referee Ashley Klein in Auckland as embarrassing, with the NRL investigating.
stories.body:
The NRL has been urged to come down hard on supporters who peppered referee Ashley Klein with projectiles as the league's integrity unit investigates the ugly aftermath of Newcastle's semifinal win over the Warriors.

Vision from Eden Park after fulltime in the Knights' 12-10 victory showed Klein being hit with a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish as he walked from the field.

The footage shows Klein having to be protected by security, as fans abused the veteran referee and projectiles rained down on him.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of their spectators' code of conduct. An Integrity Unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chairman Peter V'landys told AAP.

V'landys' no-nonsense stance was welcomed by the referee's union, Professional Rugby League Match Officials (PRLMO), who called on the NRL to come down hard on the Warriors supporters.

"The safety of all referees and match officials is paramount, and they should be allowed to perform their duties without being placed in harm's way," PRLMO chair John Choueifate told AAP.

"To say I was disappointed is an understatement and call on the NRL to investigate the incident which detracted from an enthralling match.

"They need to send a very clear message to those responsible and to others in future that this rubbish must be stamped out of the game."

New Zealand Police confirmed no arrests were made, with "no issues to note" other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors did not respond to AAP requests for comment.

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the biggest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the game from the Warriors' traditional Mt Smart Stadium home.

The NRL's investigation came as they admitted Klein had erred with a crucial decision not to penalise Newcastle prop Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Had it been awarded, the Warriors could have levelled at 12-12 and sent the game to extra time. It's understood Klein will be dropped for the preliminary finals.

Regardless, Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at fans, labelling their behaviour as "embarrassing" and said a missed call was no excuse for that reaction.

"Ashley Klein is a human being in the middle of a park doing one of the toughest jobs there is," Johnson said on his Instagram.

"In what world do we think that is okay? You guys are so quick to point out that athletes and ex-athletes are role models for your kids.

"Well you're not setting the bar very high if that's what they've got to look up to. Be better man.

"It's such a s--- way to finish a season. Not just from a result standpoint. But leaving such a sour taste from a fan base. A fan base I deeply care about."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster had vented his frustration in the postmatch press conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

The incident comes after AFL umpires also had cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG after Hawthorn's tight loss to Brisbane in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has also condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

stories.headline: UFC 331 results: Van dominates Pantoja to retain men's flyweight title
stories.summary: Joshua Van and Arman Tsarukyan earned big wins on a contender for fight card of the year. Here are the UFC 331 highlights.
stories.body:
If there were any doubts about Joshua Van's championship mettle, they were put to bed after his dominant victory over Alexandre Pantoja in the UFC 331 main event at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Saturday night.

Van outstruck Pantoja and successfully defended double-digit takedown attempts and even dropped Pantoja in Round 5 en route to a unanimous decision win to retain the UFC men's flyweight title over the former champion.

Pantoja put up a good fight, as he held his own on the feet and racked up nearly 10 minutes of control time. His best showings were in Rounds 1 and 4, when he got a hold of Van and successfully took the fight to the mat. But Van did enough to get a win on the judges' scorecards. He has now defended his title twice.

In the co-main event, Arman Tsarukyan earned what could be the biggest win of his career, putting knockout artist Mauricio Ruffy to sleep with an elbow in Round 1. The win likely cements Tsarukyan as the top contender for UFC lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.

Also on the main card, heavyweight Sean Sharaf pulled off an all-time UFC upset, knocking out top prospect Gable Steveson in just 12 seconds.

Brett Okamoto, Jeff Wagenheim and Dre Waters break down all the action from Los Angeles.

stories.headline: Antoine Semenyo happy to lead Man City's attack if needed
stories.summary: Antoine Semenyo is ready to take on the challenge of leading Manchester City's attack if needed.
stories.body:
Antoine Semenyo is ready to take on the challenge of leading Manchester City's attack if needed.

The Ghana international underlined his finishing ability with two clinical strikes in City's thrilling 5-3 victory over Sunderland in the Premier League on Sunday.

The prolific output of Erling Haaland, who was also on target as Enzo Maresca's side maintained their 100% start to the campaign, means City are rarely short of goals.

But the club's summer transfer activity has left them with no clear replacement for Haaland should the Norwegian miss any games.

Maresca has identified winger Semenyo as the most obvious alternative and the 26-year-old would be happy to step up.

Semenyo said: "I've heard about his backup striker thing. I don't know where it's come from!

"But, yes, if I need to, then I'll do it. I've no problem in doing that."

Of his finishing, he added: "I think that just comes naturally.

"Once I'm in front of the goal, I know it doesn't move. So as long as I hit it in the corner, hit it with a good connection, I know it will go in."

City were pushed all the way by Sunderland, who showed no sign of weariness from their midweek Europa League outing.

Brian Brobbey scored a hat trick for the visitors but Semenyo's double and Haaland's late effort completed the job for City, for whom Enzo Fernández and Rayan Cherki also struck.

Both sides had numerous other chances in a frantic game. Haaland missed an open goal for City while Brobbey hit the bar and Rúben Dias had to clear off the line. Sunderland also felt they should have had a penalty for handball against Elliot Anderson.

Semenyo said: "It was a tough one. Physically, we knew it would be like that -- duels, aerial balls, set-pieces.

"We knew it would be a fight, and we just needed to stick together collectively and win our individual duels and get three points, which we've done.

"Sometimes it is going to be like that, not every game you can control. You just have to ride the waves. We knew if we got our chances, we would score."

- Erling Haaland sets unique goal milestone as Man City beat Sunderland

- Enzo Maresca relieved as Manchester City pass difficult Sunderland test

City have now won seven games in succession in all competitions since their defeat by Arsenal in the Community Shield.

With a three-point lead at the top of the Premier League, it has been a strong start under new manager Maresca but Semenyo feels there is still room for improvement yet.

He said: "Everyone feels good. It's where we want to be, but we're not going to get too complacent, too relaxed. We know that there's a lot more games to go.

"We just want to continue winning, we just have to keep going.

"It's seven or eight weeks we've been together now, so it's not been too long, but we're doing well. We're winning our games and we'll keep improving."

stories.headline: The stat that could swing every NBA team's 2026-27 season
stories.summary: Let's dive into the trends, storylines and statistical nuggets that could define the NBA season.
stories.body:
One of my favorite annual preseason traditions is to identify one number for every NBA team, sourced from a variety of data points and statistical categories, that highlights a key aspect of each squad entering the new season.

Last year, for instance, this exercise foreshadowed Jalen Johnson's breakout in Atlanta, the Milwaukee Bucks' struggles in Giannis Antetokounmpo's final season and the Portland Trail Blazers' league-worst turnover rate.

Let's dive into this year's 30 numbers to get a sense for the 2026-27 season to come, featuring all sorts of trends, storylines and statistical nuggets to monitor over the next 10 months.

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NY | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks: 108.6
The Hawks allowed just 108.6 points per 100 possessions after the All-Star break, ranking second in the NBA in that span, behind only the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Over the whole season, the Hawks ranked 10th on defense -- and that was before they added Luguentz Dort, one of the most ferocious perimeter defenders in the NBA. Whether Dort and Dyson Daniels can survive on offense if and when they play together remains to be seen, but that duo with Nickeil Alexander-Walker plus Atlanta's other defensive infrastructure could combine to form one of the NBA's stingiest units.

Boston Celtics: 4
In all four of Joe Mazzulla's seasons as Boston's head coach, the Celtics have finished with a top-five offensive and defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass. Only three other squads in that span have accomplished that feat: the 2023-24 Thunder, the 2024-25 Thunder and the 2025-26 San Antonio Spurs.

That consistent two-way excellence hasn't always translated to the playoffs. In those four seasons, Boston won one title but was upset in the other three years

Yet after an offseason of turmoil, that consistency should also be encouraging for Celtics fans. Even without Jaylen Brown, their team will likely look like a championship contender on both sides once again -- in the regular season, at least.

Brooklyn Nets: 72%
Egor Demin was by far the best of the Nets' rookies last season, averaging 10.3 points per game and a solid assist-to-turnover ratio while making 38.5% of his 3-pointers. That latter statistic is especially encouraging for a player with shooting questions entering the NBA.

But Demin didn't find many ways to score other than 3-pointers, as 72% of his shot attempts last season were 3s. That was the 16th-highest rate out of 279 players with at least 1,000 minutes last season -- the three players immediately ahead of him were shooting specialists Klay Thompson, Gary Trent Jr. and Landry Shamet.

As a 6-foot-8 point guard, Demin should be more of a multidimensional scorer, even if that one dimension is so effective. The Nets will have more offensive talent next to him this season -- they drafted Mikel Brown Jr. and traded for Julius Randle -- and they'd surely love to see Demin expand his offensive repertoire to take the next step as an NBA player.

Charlotte Hornets: 11.6
The Hornets scored 125.0 points per 100 possessions when LaMelo Ball was on the floor last season, per Cleaning the Glass, which ranked in the 97th percentile of all offensive lineups leaguewide. But with Ball off the court, that number plummeted to 113.4 points per 100 possessions, or the 36th percentile.

That gap of 11.6 points was the second largest among all rotation players, sandwiching Ball between Nikola Jokic (with a 15.2-point gap) and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (an 11.0-point gap), the top two finishers in MVP voting.

The likes of Coby White, Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller could step up in Ball's stead after he departed in a surprising summer trade. But there might also be some severe growing pains for Charlotte's offense, which took the league by storm in the second half of last season but now must reorient itself around a new set of leaders.

Chicago Bulls: 42
In "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy," the number 42 is the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything. In Chicago, it's the combined age of Matas Buzelis (who will turn 22 years old next month, before opening night) and Caleb Wilson (20) -- who might as well be the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything for the Bulls, because their future rests on the development of this young frontcourt duo.

Cleveland Cavaliers: 14.2
The Cavaliers' defense slipped to a league-average 15th last season, after four consecutive seasons in the top 10. One chief culprit was the 3-point line, as opponents sank 14.2 long-range shots per game -- the fifth-highest tally in the league.

Put another way, the Cavaliers made just 10 more 3-pointers than their opponents across the 2025-26 regular season. In 2024-25, they made 199 more 3s than their opponents.

That increase was partially the result of bad luck, as opponents' 3-point percentage against Cleveland was also the fifth-highest mark in the NBA. But it was also the result of a change in shot diet. The Cavaliers ranked 22nd in opponent 3-point attempt rate last season, per Cleaning the Glass, after placing in the top 10 in every previous season of the Evan Mobley era.

Importing Peyton Watson as their top perimeter stopper could improve the Cavaliers' effectiveness while defending the arc next season, but they'll need a group effort to reverse that worrisome trend.

Dallas Mavericks: 3
Cooper Flagg will celebrate his 20th birthday in December. Only three previous players have made an All-NBA team at that age: Kobe Bryant, LeBron James and former Maverick Luka Doncic.

Flagg has a chance to join that elite company after a scorching finish to last season that won him the Rookie of the Year award. To be clear, there wouldn't be any shame if he failed to elevate to a top-15 player by his second season; there are many more 21-year-olds who made an All-NBA team for the first time, including Jayson Tatum, Anthony Davis, Kevin Durant, Dwight Howard, Carmelo Anthony and Tracy McGrady this century.

But Flagg is such a special prospect that he could conceivably follow in the footsteps of the last young Mavericks great and become one of the best players in the NBA before he is old enough to buy a beer.

Denver Nuggets: 4
According to the advanced stat estimated plus-minus, only four Nuggets rate as above-average players at this point in their careers. To be fair, that quartet -- consisting of Nikola Jokic, Jamal Murray, Aaron Gordon and Cameron Johnson -- is generally way above-average. Jokic, for instance, is the second-most-valuable player in the league by EPM's reckoning, behind only Victor Wembanyama.

But the dearth of quality supporting role players poses a real problem for Denver entering the 2026-27 season. EPM pegs Peyton Watson as an above-average player, but he's in Cleveland now. And the Nuggets' other highest-rated reserves from last season -- Jonas Valanciunas and Tim Hardaway Jr. -- also left Denver this summer. (Fifth starter Christian Braun is exactly average, per EPM.)

Among Western Conference teams, only the Kings, Clippers and Jazz have fewer above-average players than the Nuggets, while the Grizzlies and Lakers have four each as well. Denver already has a perennial tendency to struggle when Jokic is off the court, and now its bench looks weaker than ever.

Detroit Pistons: 6
Along with Cade Cunningham, Ausar Thompson and Jalen Duren seem like two of the Pistons' three great building blocks -- assuming Duren signs a long-term deal rather than taking the qualifying offer. That's why it's so notable, and so potentially concerning, that Thompson and Duren made six combined 3-pointers last season.

Thompson went 6-for-24 (25%), while Duren hasn't ever made an NBA 3, nor even attempted one in two years. Their reluctance to shoot from the perimeter is largely why Detroit finished 29th in 3-point attempts and 28th in makes.

The Pistons tried to address that weakness by adding Isaiah Joe and John Collins this summer; their hope is that the rest of the rotation can shoot enough to make up for Thompson and Duren. But their long-term fit will remain in question until both players feel comfortable spacing the floor, and they remove some of the Pistons' roster flexibility because there isn't room for any more non-shooters. Fellow youngster Ron Holland II, for instance, could be jettisoned because he's also a mere 25% shooter from deep.

Golden State Warriors: 2019
The 2018-19 season was the Warriors' last with Kevin Durant, and their last of five consecutive years with a Finals trip. It was also, to this day, the last season in which Golden State finished with a top-10 rating on both offense and defense, per Cleaning the Glass. Even in 2021-22, when the Warriors won the title, their offense ranked a distant 17th.

Typically, championship contenders rank in the top 10 on both sides, but the Warriors' lengthy drought in this category exposes one of their chief problems sustaining their superlative success in this decade: They haven't been able to find enough capable two-way players. Instead, they've had to juggle offensive standouts (e.g., Jordan Poole) and defensive specialists (e.g., Gary Payton II) without enough connective tissue between the two.

Golden State's 2026-27 roster is almost entirely the same as the injury-riddled group that stumbled to a 37-45 record last season. Better health could make them a winning team again. But they need better players if they want to reemerge as true contenders.

Houston Rockets: 37.4%
The Rockets led the NBA by grabbing 37.4% of their own misses last season, per Cleaning the Glass. According to Stathead, they had the highest offensive rebounding rate for any team since 2003.

That singular advantage buoyed an otherwise unremarkable offense. The Rockets finished seventh in offensive rating despite a below-average placement in the other most important offensive stats: They didn't shoot well on their first chances, they didn't generate free throws and they committed far too many turnovers.

However, depending so much on second chances meant the Rockets were vulnerable to offensive outages once those opportunities dried up -- as they did more often following Steven Adams' season-ending ankle injury.

In 2026-27, Houston should benefit from Fred VanVleet's return, and Kevin Durant -- who played just one game in the playoffs -- remains a tremendous offensive force. But the Rockets must find more ways to manufacture points than simply trusting that a backup center will clean up their misses when he's on the court.

Indiana Pacers: 487
When Tyrese Haliburton takes the floor for the Pacers' first game of the season -- in New Orleans rather than at home in Indiana, controversially -- 487 days will have passed since his last contest (Game 7 of the 2025 Finals).

The Pacers' season will swing based on how well Haliburton recovered and rehabilitated his torn Achilles in those 487 days. The team's supporting cast looks strong, and its system is ready to roll. But without a fully healthy Haliburton, the Pacers will resemble a sleek, speedy car without an engine.

LA Clippers: 30
The Clippers were the NBA's oldest team last season, with an average age of 30.0 years. They were also the oldest team in 2024-25 and in 2023-24, and the second-oldest in 2022-23.

And even with 30-somethings Kawhi Leonard and James Harden now gone, and 40-something Chris Paul retired, the Clippers still project as one of the NBA's older teams this season. They'll feature Brook Lopez (38), Bradley Beal (33), Kris Dunn (32), Max Strus (30), Derrick Jones Jr. (29) and Brandon Ingram (29).

Or, at least they'll project that way if they don't trade the likes of Lopez, Dunn, Strus and Jones, who would all be better suited as role players on winning teams while returning some draft capital to the Clippers. A veteran-heavy team should be trying to win now, but the Clippers aren't in that position, so they could once again be one of the most active teams before the trade deadline.

Los Angeles Lakers: 54.6%
New Lakers center Walker Kessler is one of the most important X factors in the entire NBA this season, after his team committed so much -- in terms of both money and draft capital -- to acquire him in a sign-and-trade. The Lakers went all-in on Kessler because they believe he's the missing piece who can serve as Luka Doncic's pick-and-roll partner on offense and an anchor on defense.

Kessler remains relatively untested at the NBA level after four seasons toiling away for the noncompetitive Jazz, but his rim protection numbers are pristine. Over the course of his career, he ranks third (behind Chet Holmgren and Victor Wembanyama, among players with at least 500 shots defended) by holding opponents to just 54.6% accuracy in the restricted area when he's the closest defender, per GeniusIQ.

The Lakers will rely on Kessler's individual deterrence, as the rest of their roster is light on defensive talent. He'll need to play like Rudy Gobert, who has been such a stout back-line defender throughout his career that he has allowed his teams to get away with playing offense-first players at other positions.

Incidentally, Gobert's career rim protection number, per GeniusIQ, is very close to Kessler's: 54.1%. Also incidentally, Kessler, as a recent draft pick, was part of the large package that Minnesota traded to Utah for Gobert back in 2022.

Memphis Grizzlies: 31
Across the 2021-22 and 2022-23 seasons, the Grizzlies won a combined 107 games, and they landed the West's No. 2 seed both years. Only three years have passed since then, but all 31 players who suited up for the Grizzlies in that brief successful span are now gone. Not a single player remains from those winning squads.

Most notably, Memphis has traded Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane in the last 15 months, completely resetting its competitive timetable and restocking its draft stash. Some new building blocks are already on the team -- Cameron Boozer, Cedric Coward -- and Memphis can only hope they eventually offer more sustained success than the previous core.

Miami Heat: 20
The 2025-26 Miami Heat played offense unlike any other team in modern NBA history. For instance, they set just 20 picks per 100 possessions, per GeniusIQ. In the tracking era (which began in 2013-14), the second-lowest pick frequency is from the 2018-19 76ers, at 38 picks per 100 possessions -- nearly twice as high as Miami's average.

Conversely, despite a lack of on-ball star talent, Miami ran 35 isolations per 100 possessions last season, which is the second-highest mark on record. Only the 2019-20 Rockets, led by isolation master James Harden at his peak, used that play type more frequently.

More broadly, the average team in the tracking era has 54 more picks than isolations, per 100 possessions. But the Heat flipped that relationship in the opposite direction: They had 15 more isos than picks, as the only team on record with more of the former than the latter.

On this graph showing the pick and isolation frequency from every team in the tracking era, the Heat are all alone on an island.

One of the most interesting strategic questions of the coming season is whether Miami sticks with that unique scheme now that Giannis Antetokounmpo is on the team, or if they instead shift back in the direction of a more traditional pick-and-roll-based attack.

Milwaukee Bucks: 11
For each of the past 11 seasons, Giannis Antetokounmpo has led the Bucks in value over replacement player, per Basketball-Reference. That streak will come to an end this season after his offseason trade to Miami.

Now the Bucks are searching for a new star, after more than a decade revolving around their last one. For context on how long they've been reliant on Antetokounmpo, the following players were in the rotation for the last Bucks team that didn't have him as its most valuable player: Brandon Knight, Zaza Pachulia, Ersan Ilyasova, Larry Sanders, Michael Carter-Williams, Jared Dudley and O.J. Mayo.

Minnesota Timberwolves: 6,008
The Timberwolves' acquisition of LaMelo Ball means they now have the No. 1 and No. 3 picks from the 2020 draft in their backcourt: Anthony Edwards and Ball, respectively. Both players are All-Stars with incredible shooting range and a flair for highlight plays in transition.

But among other differences -- such as Edwards' two conference finals trips, contrasted with zero playoff games for Ball -- one important gap separates the players' NBA trajectories thus far: Edwards has played 6,008 more regular-season minutes than his new teammate. That's the equivalent of roughly 200 extra games at a starter's workload.

Part of that disparity stems from Ball's frequent injury issues, as he's exceeded 47 games just once in the last four seasons. Another part stems from the Hornets' cautious usage of Ball to keep him on the court; he averaged only 28 minutes per game last season, which helped him play 72 games.

Yet the Timberwolves might not have the depth to engage in considerable load management practices with the 25-year-old Ball, and in any event, they might not want to, after pinning their short- and long-term hopes on his ability to pair with Edwards. When the two guards play together, the Timberwolves should thrive, but it's unclear just how often that will be, given Ball's history.

New Orleans Pelicans: Negative-12.3
When Zion Williamson and Derik Queen shared the floor last season, the Pelicans were outscored by 12.3 points per 100 possessions. That net rating ranked in the 12th percentile of all lineups, per Cleaning the Glass. In those alignments, the Pelicans struggled to score (18th percentile) and defend (12th percentile). They were miserable all around.

That's a problem going forward because Williamson and Queen are arguably the Pelicans' most important player and most important prospect, respectively, yet their skill sets overlap too much -- they're both big creators with no shooting range and defensive vulnerabilities -- to work together. This season will be a crucial test of whether they can function any better given more time to develop.

For now, if the Pelicans want to continue building around Williamson, it's hard to envision Queen getting sufficient playing time to develop. Yet if they want to build around Queen, then they might have to move their former No. 1 pick for the good of the team over the long term.

New York Knicks: 14.9
The Knicks set a record with a plus-14.9 point differential in the playoffs, which was the highest mark for any champion in NBA history. Six of the seven previous leaders in this stat went on to repeat as champions the following season.

Granted, all of those teams were much better in the regular season than the 53-29 Knicks, which is one reason New York's playoff burst was so extraordinary and unexpected. There might not be the same sort of carryover with the Knicks as with the other teams in that chart.

But it's not hard to dream that the Knicks' true talent is closer to what they showed in the playoffs than in the past few regular seasons. History is on their side as they attempt to become the NBA's first repeat champion in nine years.

Oklahoma City Thunder: 33%
In the 2024-25 regular season, when the Thunder went 68-14 and set a point differential record en route to the championship, they won 83% of their games.

In 2025-26, counting both regular season and playoffs, they did slightly better by winning 84% of their games -- if you don't count their 4-8 record against the Spurs.

But those 12 games at a 33% winning percentage -- 1-4 in the regular season, 3-4 in the conference finals -- were the most important of the Thunder's season, as they prevented Oklahoma City from returning to the Finals. The Thunder are such a dominant, well-rounded team that at this point, their main concern may be how to beat the Spurs rather than the other 28 teams put together. They couldn't solve that problem last season, and it should only grow harder as San Antonio's young core improves.

Orlando Magic: 2012
I've been performing this exercise for years, and Orlando's defining number has been 2012 in every edition thus far. That's because 2012 -- which was Dwight Howard's last year with the Magic -- is still the last year in which Orlando ranked in the top half of the league in offensive efficiency.

Even the addition of Desmond Bane last season couldn't boost Orlando over this stubborn hurdle, thanks to injuries and the continued awkwardness of the Paolo Banchero-Franz Wagner partnership. Perhaps new coach Sean Sweeney can finally solve this intractable issue; if not, the Magic might be forced to engage in larger roster changes next summer.

Philadelphia 76ers: 55.8%
According to GeniusIQ, the 76ers defense allowed a shot quality of 55.8% last season, meaning their opponents would have been expected to finish with a 55.8% effective field goal mark, based on factors like shot location and defender distance.

That was the sixth-highest opponent shot quality in the league, behind only five tanking teams that all lost at least 56 games. In other words, Philadelphia allowed the easiest shots of any team that was trying to win games.

The 76ers' defensive outcomes weren't that disastrous because they got lucky: Their opponents' actual eFG% underperformed their expected eFG% by the most of any team. But even with that luck, they still finished just 17th in defensive rating, which is below the level of a team with Finals aspirations.

Much of the focus on Philadelphia's championship chances this season has centered on offense, where Nick Nurse must figure out how to integrate Jaylen Brown and LeBron James with the 76ers' incumbent stars. But greater issues will likely arise on the other end, where they're hoping that Brown and Dean Wade can help what was quietly a major problem last season.

Phoenix Suns: 34%
Here are last season's 3-point percentages for the Suns' projected starters:

Devin Booker: 33%

Jalen Green: 31%

Dillon Brooks: 34%

Miles Bridges: 33%

Oso Ighodaro: 0% (one attempt)

The highest mark among that group is Brooks' 34%, which is still below league average. Meanwhile, Booker has been stuck at 33% for two seasons now, Green has never been above 35% in any season, and Bridges has exceeded that mark just once (in 2020-21).

Collin Gillespie is a very good shooter (40% last season) off the bench -- and he very well might need to enter the starting lineup eventually to provide more spacing -- but losing Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale in the Bridges trade could cost Phoenix dearly. The Suns were a surprising success story last season, but they might not have enough spacing to repeat in 2026-27.

Portland Trail Blazers: 27.7
Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was the king of drives in the NBA. Entering last year, he'd led all starters in drives per 100 possessions, according to GeniusIQ, for five straight seasons, dating back to his first year as Oklahoma City's primary ball-handler.

But that streak ended last season, when Deni Avdija averaged 27.7 drives per 100 possessions to usurp SGA's crown. (Jaylen Brown also edged out Gilgeous-Alexander, knocking him down to third place.) That was a massive increase in usage for Avdija, who'd averaged 17.3 drives just a year earlier.

It was also undeniably effective: Avdija averaged 1.11 points per drive, which ranked in the 72nd percentile among high-usage drivers. He was a first-time All-Star and finished 16th -- or, the first runner-up -- in All-NBA voting.

Yet now Avdija will share a court with a couple of ball-dominant guards in Damian Lillard and Ja Morant. Among the many questions about how Portland's new backcourt will function, one of the most interesting is whether the Trail Blazers' best player will continue to thrive if he doesn't have as many opportunities to get to the basket.

Sacramento Kings: 83
The Kings' five projected starters played just 83 combined games for the team last year. Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Keegan Murray were injured for the majority of the season. De'Andre Hunter played just two games after a deadline trade before suffering an injury of his own. And rookie Darius Acuff Jr., of course, was playing in college rather than Sacramento.

This data point isn't meant to suggest that the Kings will be good this season. But it's at least worth noting that their disastrous 60-loss campaign in 2025-26 was partly the result of losing almost all of their best players early on.

San Antonio Spurs: 17.0
The Spurs posted a plus-17.0 net rating with Victor Wembanyama on the floor last year, per NBA Advanced Stats. That was the second-best mark among all rotation players, and the only one in the top six that didn't belong to a Thunder player: Alex Caruso led the league in this stat, followed by Wembanyama, Gilgeous-Alexander, Chet Holmgren, Ajay Mitchell and Isaiah Hartenstein.

In other words, while the Thunder might have the best collective team by the numbers, the Spurs enter that conversation because of Wembanyama's singular talents and impact. And he is already at that level despite being 22 years old, with theoretically much more improvement still ahead of him. As long as he can stay healthy, the Spurs should remain leading title contenders for many years to come.

Toronto Raptors: 14.4
When Kawhi Leonard was on the court last season, the LA Clippers were 14.4 points better per 100 possessions than when he was off. That was the third-best margin among all players with at least 1,500 minutes, per Cleaning the Glass.

Conversely, when Brandon Ingram was on the court last season, the Raptors were 9.0 points worse per 100 possessions than when he was off. That was the third-worst margin among that group.

And now Toronto has replaced Ingram with Leonard via an offseason trade, thereby replacing a low-impact player with one of the perennially highest-impact players in the league. This stat alone is enough to show Toronto's upside as a championship contender this year.

Utah Jazz: 31
Over Will Hardy's four-year tenure as Utah's coach, after he took over following the dismantling of the Rudy Gobert/Donovan Mitchell/Quin Snyder playoff squad, the Jazz rank 29th in cumulative win percentage. But they've arrived in a strange way: They've won at a 31-51 pace before the All-Star break, but a 17-65 pace afterward.

That disparity reflects how Utah has tended to approach recent seasons -- typically with a surprisingly competitive start, followed by a furious race to the bottom of the standings (and the top of the draft). Now that the Jazz have turned a corner toward competitiveness once again, highlighted by last season's Jaren Jackson Jr. trade, it will be fascinating to see how Hardy approaches a season when he's actually trying to win for all 82 games.

This stat also suggests that the Jazz aren't really attempting to climb from the caliber of a 60-loss team to the playoffs all at once. They were more often a run-of-the-mill bad team until engaging in tank mode come March and April.

Washington Wizards: 3.3%
The Wizards pulled off a dreadful double last season: According to Second Spectrum, they had the lowest shot quality of any team on offense, and they allowed the highest shot quality of any team on defense.

On average, every shot from a Wizards opponent had a 3.3% higher expected effective field goal percentage than every shot from the Wizards themselves. That gap was so wide that the 29th-place team by this metric (the Grizzlies) was as far away from 21st place as from the Wizards in the 30th.

Adding Trae Young for more than the five games he played for Washington last season should help the offense generate better shots, and adding Anthony Davis should help the defense force tougher looks. No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa could help on both ends. The only way out from last place is upward, after all.

But if Washington has any dreams of playoff contention with its new stars, this statistic should serve as a sobering reminder of just how far the Wizards have to go. Star power alone won't fix all the big process problems that plagued Washington last season.

stories.headline: No decision made on banned five's future, say Swans
stories.summary: Zach Merrett has spoken glowingly of new Essendon coach Mark McVeigh amid rampant speculation that he will bid again for an AFL trade to Hawthorn.
stories.body:
Sydney's five exiled players have yet to be welcomed back to the AFL club amid speculation the Swans will reintegrate the suspended group.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon have been absent from Swans headquarters since being suspended in August.

The five were stood down for breaching club standards following a postmatch party at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate from a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid, and AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

As the Swans head into exit meetings following last Friday's preliminary final loss to Fremantle, AFL.com.au reported on Monday the five were expected to return to the club this week.

But Swans chief executive Pavlich, speaking later on Monday before the Brownlow Medal count, said no decision on the five's reintegration had been made.

"We haven't confirmed that as yet. We're still working through the process," Pavlich told AAP.

"They're five of our players, five contracted players, people we've tried to support through this process.

"Their wellbeing, along with everyone impacted, has been at the forefront of our mind.

"So we'll continue to work through that."

All five are contracted for next year, with Blakey signed to the club until 2031.

Warner and Jordon come off contract at the end of 2027, while Heeney and Bice are signed until the end of 2028.

Blakey is reportedly seeking a trade to Victorian rivals, but football boss Leon Cameron has dismissed those rumblings as "speculation".

Victoria Police's eight-week timeline prediction on their probe of the Pullman Hotel incident -- which was first flagged on September 2 -- takes in the free agency and trade period from October 2 to October 14.

Main ball-winners Heeney and Warner weren't invited to the Brownlow function at Crown Palladium, but remained eligible for the award.

Heeney and Warner are expected to be frontrunners for Sydney's Bob Skilton Medal, to be held after this Saturday's grand final.

Los Angeles Sparks (16-26, 9-12 Western Conference) at Las Vegas Aces (29-13, 15-6 Western Conference)

Las Vegas; Tuesday, 10 p.m. EDT

BOTTOM LINE: Las Vegas Aces will aim for its 30th win of the season when the Aces host the Los Angeles Sparks.

The Aces are 15-6 in conference play. Las Vegas has a 3-2 record in games decided by 3 points or fewer.

The Sparks are 9-12 in Western Conference play. Los Angeles gives up 91.7 points to opponents while being outscored by 4.2 points per game.

Las Vegas' average of 8.6 made 3-pointers per game this season is just 0.4 fewer made shots on average than the 9.0 per game Los Angeles gives up. Los Angeles averages 87.5 points per game, 1.4 more than the 86.1 Las Vegas allows.

The teams square off for the fourth time this season. The Aces won the last meeting 79-69 on June 3, with A'ja Wilson scoring 25 points in the victory.

Nneka Ogwumike is averaging 17.3 points, 8.9 rebounds and 3.1 assists for the Sparks. Dearica Hamby is averaging 10.4 points over the last 10 games.

LAST 10 GAMES: Aces: 7-3, averaging 90.3 points, 31.6 rebounds, 20.5 assists, 7.7 steals and 4.5 blocks per game while shooting 46.5% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 83.5 points per game.

Sparks: 4-6, averaging 82.4 points, 30.7 rebounds, 21.4 assists, 8.8 steals and 4.2 blocks per game while shooting 45.6% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 85.7 points.

stories.headline: Azerbaijan Grand Prix 2026: Race start time in Baku, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 is heading to the streets of Baku for this year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix as we roll into the business end of the season.
stories.body:
Formula 1 is heading to the streets of Baku for this year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix as we roll into the business end of the season.

Title leader Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the drivers' championship after picking up his eighth victory of the season at the brand-new Madring last time out.

He leads his teammate George Russell by 81 points, with Lewis Hamilton now dropping back in the title race after a retirement in Spain.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 15th race of the season.

- Madring's F1 debut left everyone dissatisfied, even Spanish GP's top 3

- Max Verstappen wins Max vs 100 in style after overtaking 100 go-karters in 35 minutes

- F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule

Azerbaijan Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Thursday, September 24

Practice One: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Practice Two: 1 p.m. - 2 p.m.

Friday, September 25

Final Practice: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Qualifying: 1 p.m. - 2 p.m.

Saturday, September 26

Azerbaijan Grand Prix: 12 p.m.

How to watch

Sky Sports has exclusive F1 rights again in 2026 in the U.K., with every session live on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Why is the race on a Saturday?
For the first time in Baku's history, the F1 weekend will shift a day forwards, with the race taking place on a Saturday to avoid a clash with an Azerbaijan National Day of mourning on the Sunday.

Azerbaijan's people will dedicate their thoughts to military personnel and those who died during the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.

Baku City Circuit

After the European leg of the calendar where circuits are more traditional, Baku is one of the standout street circuits of the season.

The first race in Baku was held in 2016 as the European Grand Prix before it was called the Azerbaijan Grand Prix a year later.

The section around Turns 8, 9 and 10 are lined by the walls of the city's charming old town including a castle and the long main straight along the Baku shoreline sees cars reach speeds in excess of 220 mph and is the best spot for overtaking.

The walls are narrow and the high-speeds make for either a race full of chaos, or none at all. There is a 57% chance of a Safety Car being deployed during the race.

Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Circuit: Baku City Circuit; Baku, Azerbaijan

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2017: Daniel Ricciardo (Red Bull)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes)

2021: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2022: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2024: Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2016 European GP. (First race as Azerbaijan GP in 2017)

Laps: 51 laps of 6km.

Lap record: 1:43.009, Charles Leclerc (2019).

Most wins: Pérez (2021, 2023) and Verstappen (2022, 2025) with two wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Hamilton (2018), Bottas (2019) and Piastri (2024).

Most poles: Leclerc with four (2021-2024) and Hamilton (2017), Bottas (2019) and Verstappen (2025) are the other pole sitters from the current grid.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be dry and sunny throughout the weekend. Temperatures will be around 26°C, but will drop to 24°C for the race on Saturday.

What happened last year?
Red Bull's Verstappen took pole position around the streets of Baku in a qualifying session that featured a record six red flags.

He ended up converting that pole into a dominant victory, with Russell in second and Carlos Sainz behind.

It was a key moment in the championship fight between Lando Norris and Piastri as Norris closed the gap to 25 points to his McLaren teammate after the Australian crashed out.

Who will win this year?

The last street circuit this year was in Monaco in June and since then several of the top teams have upgraded its packages and haven't yet gone racing on street circuits, but Baku has now arrived.

Antonelli has looked on fire in the last two races, but Norris is creeping to the front. The reigning world champion has two wins to his name in Hungary and Zandvoort, but also suffered an unlucky run in Madrid with the safety car deployment, so missed out on a potential win there as well.

Mercedes are set to be quick in the high-speed straight lines in Baku, but the tight and twisty corners might suit Ferrari and McLaren best.

One of the main aims will be to not crash the car into the wall otherwise the whole course of the race can rapidly change in a blink of an eye.
